item.title: A Universal Constitutive Relation for Static Droplet Retention
item.description: arXiv:2610.33100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under applied forcing, static droplet retention is accompanied by contact angle asymmetry, with unequal apparent contact angles on opposite sides. Yet, the relation between the asymmetry and forcing lacks a common constitutive basis. Here, we show that the asymmetry emerges from minimizing the forcing-dependent free energy. The response of the asymmetry to forcing defines a susceptibility whose zero-forcing value yields a universal constitutive relation between the asymmetry and forcing. The constitutive relation is quantitatively validated across liquids, volumes, and forcing levels.
item.dc:creator: Lisen Bi, Fei Wang, Ruize Yin, Britta Nestler

item.title: Spatial symmetry invariance of three-dimensional Navier-Stokes turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2610.33115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) of the deterministic Navier-Stokes (NS) equations is widely used to provide benchmark solutions of turbulent flow, but its accuracy and reliability have not been rigorously inspected from a mathematical viewpoint. Here we prove a spatial symmetry invariance theorem (SSIT) of three-dimensional NS equations whereby an exact solution of deterministic NS equations under periodic boundary conditions maintains the same spatial symmetry as its symmetric initial flow, forever. SSIT provides an absolute benchmark test for computational fluid dynamics (CFD). It is shown herein that traditional DNS of NS turbulence quickly violates SSIT, revealing that the spatiotemporal trajectory of NS turbulence predicted by DNS soon becomes badly polluted by numerical noise. Importantly, it is found that even the statistical results of DNS might be unstable, i.e., exhibit sensitivity dependence on the initial flow conditions. In other words, the loss of spatial symmetry in traditional DNS of NS turbulence is not a physical instability but instead a numerical artifact caused by the chaotic nature of the flow. Using the SSIT, it is straightforward to deduce several key properties of NS turbulence, including `ultra-chaos', the so-called `noise-expansion cascade', `permanent memory of symmetric initial flow conditions', and so on. Note that permanent memory of symmetric initial flow conditions suggests that NS turbulence governed by deterministic NS equations subject to symmetric initial flow should have no `mixing', corresponding to non-ergodicity, although ergodicity is one of the most fundamental assumptions of turbulence theory.
item.dc:creator: Shijun Liao

item.title: Flow Mesh: A Velocity-Regularized Flow Matching Framework for Stable Distributional Modeling of Physical Fields on Unstructured Meshes
item.description: arXiv:2610.33204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermal-fluid field distributions underpin the analysis and operation of energy infrastructure, from nuclear-reactor cooling channels to industrial heat exchangers, but resolving these distributions through computational fluid dynamics requires prohibitively large simulation ensembles. Their complex geometries also demand unstructured meshes that are poorly accommodated by generative models developed for regular grids. Here we introduce FlowMesh, a generative framework that combines permutation-invariant mesh encoding with deterministic latent flow matching and an l1 penalty on the learned transport velocity. FlowMesh generates full-field realizations directly on fixed unstructured meshes without auxiliary grid interpolation or a stochastic denoising chain. Across lid-driven-cavity, pressurized-water-reactor subchannel and heat-exchanger datasets, evaluated over six matched training seeds, FlowMesh achieves macro-averaged probability-density-function coverage of 91.7%-97.0%, exceeding an architecture-controlled latent diffusion model by $11.6$--$45.4$ percentage points. Latent-velocity regularization increases coverage by $3.8$ percentage points for reactor flows and 1.1 points for heat-exchanger flows, while reducing temperature-field Kullback--Leibler divergence by 1.7-2.4-fold. Each full-field realization requires 1.23 \pm 0.15 s, providing a 585--1902-fold wall-clock acceleration over computational fluid dynamics. FlowMesh therefore makes large-scale generative characterization of thermal-fluid states computationally feasible, providing a foundation for data-driven analysis and digital-twin development in fixed-geometry energy systems.
item.dc:creator: Siddharth Verma, Jaewan Park, Jay Phil Yoo, Kazuma Kobayashi, Souvik Chakraborty, Syed Bahauddin Alam

item.title: Predicting the onset of airfoil stall in transitional and turbulent flows with a pressure-gradient-based separation model for RANS simulations
item.description: arXiv:2610.33268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an improved version of the $k$-$\omega$ shear-stress transport Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes model that supersedes our prior work (Griffin et al. 2024 J. Turb.) with an updated pressure-gradient sensor that generalizes well across geometries and to laminar, transitional, and turbulent flows alike. The model is based on a composite pressure gradient criterion that uses the solution of an intermittency transport equation to synthesize the separation criteria of the Falkner-Skan theory for laminar flows and the continuously critical theory for turbulent flows. The proposed model is applied to various airfoils including the thick airfoils representative of wind turbine applications (DU00-w-212, S809 and S814) and thinner airfoils used in aerospace applications [NACA23012 and NLF(1)-0416]. For all airfoils, the proposed model is found to preserve or improve the predictions of the baseline model for both fully turbulent and transitional airfoils as demonstrated with results for the lift and drag coefficients. The model is also found to improve the prediction of separation on the NREL Phase VI rotor in a preliminary study, suggesting that the model will generalize to other complex three-dimensional flows.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Patrick Griffin, Bumseok Lee, Ganesh Vijayakumar, Benjamin Savino, Brett J. Bornhoft, Omkar B. Shende, Michael P. Whitmore

item.title: Six-Degree-of-Freedom Rotor-Load Cross-Spectral Density from Rotor-Plane Turbulence Cross-Spectra
item.description: arXiv:2610.33513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A frequency-domain response analysis of a wind turbine rotor requires the complete hub-load spectrum, but the customary scalar thrust and torque spectra retain neither the four in-plane components nor the coupling between them. This paper derives the full six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) rotor-load cross-spectral-density (CSD) matrix from the IEC Kaimal turbulence model. By decoupling the spatial order of inflow coherence from the temporal Doppler shift, the formulation introduces a two-index rotational-sampling kernel. Rotor symmetry and azimuthal averaging constrain the observed Doppler carrier strictly to blade-passing harmonics $pBf_{\mathrm{rot}}$, while the azimuthal aerodynamic transfer shifts the spatial coherence order to $pB+s$. A convergence study of the retained azimuthal order $s$ shows that $\lvert s\rvert\le4$ suffices, the assembled CSD then deviating from the full-band result by less than $10^{-5}$ in relative norm. The formulation is compared with OpenFAST simulations of a rigid floating wind turbine over nine wind speeds: the six auto-spectral densities agree closely below 1~Hz, and the present theory over-predicts the spectra near the 6P and 9P rotational harmonics.
item.dc:creator: Haoran Yang, Zhaolong Han

item.title: Energy cascades in atmospheric moist convection
item.description: arXiv:2610.33827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze scale-by-scale budgets of velocity and buoyancy second-order structure functions using Large Eddy Simulation of the BOMEX trade-wind cumulus layer. The simulation utilizes a $10\,\mathrm{m}$ grid resolution under the anelastic approximation, incorporating moist thermodynamics to capture phase changes. The analysis of derived turbulence kinetic energy (TKE) and turbulence potential energy (TPE) budgets reveals four regions of distinct turbulence dynamics. For three of these regions, approximate balances holding over wide range of length scales are identified, highlighting the importance of interspace and pressure transport. Above the lifting condensation level ($\approx 800\,\mathrm{m}$), phase changes introduce forcing across all resolved scales, leading to an inverse TPE cascade spanning all scales. The TKE, inter-scale transfer is inverse above the vertical velocity integral length scale but below the horizontal velocity scale. In the upper cloud layer ($>1400\,\mathrm{m}$), forward inter-scale transfers are recovered despite ongoing phase changes. A phenomenological interpretation of these features, referring to the different formation stages of convective updrafts, is also proposed. Finally, 1D horizontal subsamples from the simulation show good agreement with recent airborne measurements, validating the numerical framework and confirming the departure of moist convective turbulence from standard energy cascade models.
item.dc:creator: Pawe{\l} J\k{e}drejko, Marta Wac{\l}awczyk, Benjamin Luce, Szymon P. Malinowski, Jakub Nowak, J. Christos Vassilicos

item.title: Neural Eigenfluid Bases: Spectral Objectives, Gauge, and Topology
item.description: arXiv:2610.33925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reduced-order models simplify fluid simulation by representing complex flows with a small number of spatial modes. Building on Laplacian Eigenfluids, we introduce Neural Eigenfluid Bases (NEB), a neural representation whose basis functions can be evaluated anywhere in space. We enforce incompressibility and impermeable boundaries directly through differential lifts and potential boundary conditions. Geometry-local orthogonalization and Rayleigh minimization then learn an ordered basis. We connect learning in potential and velocity spaces, and derive a spectral-variance relation explaining why these objectives weight approximate modes differently, even though their exact positive spectra agree. Gauge fixing reduces the number of spatial derivatives needed for potential learning, while a Dirichlet energy loss learns independent circulation fields around obstacles. With 1024 modes, both objectives keep velocity errors below 1% in periodic vortex merger. For random flows around obstacles, potential-based learning captures more initial energy and gives lower final errors than numerical Laplacian bases of the same size. The reduced state is about a thousand times smaller than the full reference model. Three-dimensional tests separate spatial reconstruction errors from errors in coefficient evolution. Precomputed Galerkin operators allow millisecond-scale updates when the same basis is reused across simulations. This provides a physically constrained basis for continuous flow reconstruction and efficient reduced-order simulation.
item.dc:creator: Baiming Zhang, Shiying Xiong, Zhecheng Wang

item.title: Amplitude-Dependent Damping of Gravity--Capillary Waves in Power-Law Fluids: An Energy-Dissipation Framework
item.description: arXiv:2610.34351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical gravity--capillary theory locates the restoring-force crossover, but the wave amplitudes and depths for which energy losses remain measurable depend on the constitutive response and on where viscous dissipation occurs. We develop a weak-loss mechanical-energy model for small-steepness progressive surface waves in memoryless power--law liquids. The full invariant of the leading inviscid strain field yields the deep-water bulk law $\dd A/\dd t=-C_tA^n$, with $C_t=4Kk^2(2k\Omega)^{n-1}/[(n+1)\rho]$, and the corresponding spatial law $\dd A/\dd x=-(C_t/v_g)A^n$. For finite depth we calculate bulk dissipation using a phase- and depth-resolved quadrature $J_n(kh)$ and formulate a separate oscillatory power--law bottom layer. We solve the latter numerically in periodic state, obtaining dimensionless integrated wall losses $I_{0.6}\simeq0.5432$ and $I_{1.4}\simeq0.4708$ and recovering the exact Newtonian benchmark $I_1=1/2$. These values make it possible to evaluate conditional finite-depth bulk--wall dominance boundaries rather than only their amplitude exponents. The theory is organized into restoring-force, attenuation, local propagation-length, and dissipation-mechanism regime maps; at fixed wave steepness it additionally predicts a capillary-side maximum of normalized temporal damping for $0<n<2/3$. Grid, time-step, domain, and energy-work checks support the reduced wall calculation, while the coupled bulk--wall approximation still requires independent free-surface numerical or experimental validation. The results provide a reproducible single-fluid reference for subsequent two-liquid interfacial-wave modeling.
item.dc:creator: Sabbir Hassan

item.title: On Gill's problem with anomalous diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2610.35078v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classical formulation of Gill's theorem establishing the linear stability of the buoyant flow in a vertical porous channel subject to transverse diffusion and bounded by impermeable walls is here reconsidered from the perspective of anomalous mass diffusion. Anomalous diffusion is a physical effect implying a more general formulation of the governing equations of mass transfer either in a fluid or in a fluid-saturated porous medium. Anomalous diffusion is mathematically modelled via a diffusion equation with a time-dependent mass diffusivity. In this study, the stationary and parallel buoyant flow in a vertical porous layer saturated by a fluid is investigated. The implications of the anomalous diffusion model for the proof that such a flow is always linearly stable are analysed.
item.dc:creator: A. Barletta

item.title: Generative AI in Turbulence: Foundations, Applications, Validations and Benchmarks
item.description: arXiv:2610.35123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI offers new approaches to turbulence problems in which incomplete observations or unresolved d.o.f. admit multiple physically plausible solutions. Potential applications include stochastic closures, super-resolution, data assimilation, uncertainty quantification, and the generation of Eulerian and Lagrangian flow ensembles. However, turbulence is not a conventional image-generation problem. Its multiscale dynamics, intermittency, extreme events, rough velocity fields and intrinsically stochastic transport make visual realism, pointwise error, and low-order spectral agreement insufficient measures of physical fidelity. We examine where generative AI provide novel capabilities with emphasis on diffusion models, score-based methods, and related probability-transport formulations. We discuss their use in unconditional generation, probabilistic reconstruction, reduced-order modeling, temporal evolution, and mesh-free representations. We argue that validation must address turbulence properties: energy transfer, structure functions, anomalous scaling, pdf tails, coherent structures, conservation laws, temporal consistency, ensemble diversity and generalization. Finally, we discuss potential limitations in validation, baseline, data availability and reproducibility, and the need for a benchmark ecosystem combining open data, standardized challenges, hidden tests, physics-aware metrics, and documented failures. This paper serves as a bridge between two communities. For AI practitioners, we provide a fair and accessible introduction to turbulence, essential for appreciating the challenges posed by the field and for assessing the physical relevance of generative models. For turbulent practitioners, we provide an introduction to the key technological aspects of Generative AI, clarifying what these tools actually do, and where their potential and current limitations lie.
item.dc:creator: Luca Biferale, Michele Buzzicotti

item.title: Theoretical progress on regularized lattice Boltzmann collision models on weakly incompressible and compressible thermal flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.35134v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Numerical stability has long constrained the application of lattice Boltzmann methods to high-Reynolds-number and high-Mach-number flows. Improving the stability and accuracy of collision models has therefore remained a major challenge for nearly three decades. Regularized collision models constitute an important class of lattice Boltzmann collision models and have recently undergone substantial theoretical development. They are now widely used for high-Reynolds-number turbulence, high-Mach-number compressible flow and aeroacoustics. This article systematically reviews their development and establishes a unified theoretical framework that clarifies the relationships among the principal formulations. The analysis identifies the underlying principle of the regularized multiple-relaxation collision model: higher-order kinetic moments that cannot be represented by the discrete lattice are rapidly relaxed in a coordinate-independent, self-similar moment space, thereby preventing spurious modes from contaminating the hydrodynamic equations.
item.dc:creator: Xuhui Li, Xiaowen Shan, Wenyang Duan

item.title: Instability of exact finite-amplitude acoustic-gravity waves
item.description:
arXiv:2610.35210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Godin (	extit{J. Fluid Mech.}, vol. 767, 2015, pp. 52--64) showed that compressible fluids in a uniform gravity field support finite-amplitude incompressible wave motions, in which every parcel conserves pressure and density, and constructed exact Gerstner-type surface and edge waves, possibly carried by currents. Using the short-wavelength instability method for compressible flows, we show that these waves are linearly unstable above a critical steepness. The stability of each fluid level reduces to a Floquet problem depending on two parameters: the steepness $\mathfrak{e}=e^{ka_2}$ and $
u^2=(1-\mathfrak{e}^2)
u_0^2$, where $
u_0^2=\cos^2\alpha\,N_0^2/\Omega^2$, $N_0$ is the buoyancy frequency of the hydrostatic reference state, $\alpha$ the inclination of the plane of motion and $\Omega=(gk\cos\alpha)^{1/2}$ the intrinsic orbital frequency. In an isentropic fluid, a level is unstable if $\mathfrak{e}>1/3$, recovering Leblanc's threshold for Gerstner waves (	extit{J. Fluid Mech.}, vol. 506, 2004, pp. 245--254) and extending it to compressible surface and edge waves; weak stable stratification lowers the threshold to $ rac13- rac{32}{81}
u_0^2+O(
u_0^4)$. In an isothermal atmosphere, $
u_0^2=\kappa\cos\alpha/(kH)$, where $H$ is the pressure scale height. For horizontal wavelengths near $5.5\,H/\cos\alpha$, principal subharmonic resonance makes the critical steepness vanish. For the fast airglow wave observed by Hecht et al. (	extit{J. Geophys. Res.}, vol. 107, 2002, D20, 4444), which Godin interpreted with his solution, the lidar temperature places the layer in which this interpretation is consistent on this resonance, where the critical steepness is typically 0.1 instead of $1/3$. Instability is confined to a layer beneath the free surface of surface waves and to a wedge at the shoreline of edge waves.
item.dc:creator: Christian Puntini

item.title: Physics-Constrained Symbolic Regression for Mean-Velocity and Mixing-Length Scaling in Zero-Pressure-Gradient Turbulent Boundary Layers
item.description: arXiv:2610.35276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Developing interpretable full-profile relations for mean velocity and effective mixing length remains challenging because the near-wall, overlap, and outer regions exhibit distinct scaling behaviors. In this paper, physics-constrained symbolic regression is used to construct analytical relations for incompressible zero-pressure-gradient turbulent boundary layers. Classical logarithmic and Prandtl mixing-length scalings provide the starting points, while the regression identifies near-wall transition functions under asymptotic constraints and Reynolds-number-dependent outer corrections. The resulting expressions retain the prescribed leading-order near-wall exponents, reproduce the principal overlap-region behavior, and describe finite-Reynolds-number variations. The mean-velocity relation agrees well with 35 profiles from direct numerical simulations, large-eddy simulations, and experiments spanning friction Reynolds numbers from 252 to 72,526, while the mixing-length relation captures the principal trends in the simulation-derived data. These results illustrate how physical scaling knowledge can guide symbolic regression toward compact, interpretable analytical descriptions of canonical wall turbulence.
item.dc:creator: Xianglin Shan, Weiwei Zhang

item.title: From Stochastic Transport Models to High-Dimensional Bayesian Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.35352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Stochastic Transport in Upper Ocean Dynamics project introduced a new paradigm for representing uncertainty in geophysical fluid dynamics through stochastic transport models calibrated from data. This paper provides a synthesis of the principal theoretical and data assimilation developments achieved as part of the project. The central theme of the paper is the transformation of stochastic transport models from a modelling paradigm into a mathematically rigorous framework equipped with analytical, variational, calibration and Bayesian data assimilation methodologies suitable for geophysical fluid dynamics. We describe the development of the theory of stochastic transport equations, including well-posedness, regularity and approximation results, together with their geometric foundations based on stochastic variational principles, rough paths and fractional transport models. We further review methodologies for calibrating stochastic transport structures from observational and high-resolution simulation data, ranging from reduced-order stochastic models to modern generative approaches. Finally, we discuss Bayesian inference and high-dimensional data assimilation techniques developed for stochastic transport models, including particle filter methodologies and machine learning uncertainty quantification. Taken together, these developments establish a coherent framework linking stochastic transport modelling, rigorous analysis, calibration and Bayesian inference, thereby providing a foundation for uncertainty quantification and forecasting in geophysical fluid dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Dan Crisan, Oana Lang

item.title: Performance and optimization of multi-fin oscillatory propulsion
item.description: arXiv:2610.35395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-fin bioinspired propulsion systems have seen a rise in interest recently due to natural occurrence in animal systems and emerging technology. These systems make use of fin-fin interaction to improve swimming performance where the downstream fins use the wake of the upstream fin to their benefit. While 2-fin systems are relatively well understood, it is unclear how performance is impacted as the number of fins grow. Using an immersed boundary method solver, we model the multi-fin systems to analyze performance across several key parameters: spacing between fins, phase offset, freestream velocity, and number of fins per system. We characterize performance via system thrust and propulsive efficiency. We show that a dimensionless phase parameter incorporating inter-fin spacing, oscillation frequency, and freestream velocity approximately collapses the thrust response across different operating conditions, providing a useful predictor of favorable wake-interaction timing. As more fins are added ($>2$), they can further enhance the group thrust and efficiency without modifying the performance of the fins upstream. Through optimization, we found this enhancement to peak with a 3-4 fin system, after which performance diminishes with additional fins due to the growing wake complexity. Optimal conditions led to boosts in thrust or efficiency of 30% and 20%, respectively. From this study, we show that there are performance gains realized in larger fin systems (though with diminishing returns) and optimizing system performance of multi-fin systems can be done sequentially to save computational resources.
item.dc:creator: Parker T. Grobe, Ethan J. Watson, Tyler Van Buren

item.title: Thermosolutal Marangoni instabilities in a weakly viscoelastic falling film with soluble surfactant
item.description: arXiv:2610.35481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine the linear stability and nonlinear evolution of a heated falling film containing a soluble surfactant and a weakly viscoelastic liquid. The stress response is described by the short-memory Walters model, while surface tension depends on temperature and surface concentration. An Orr--Sommerfeld analysis and its long-wave limit determine how elastic memory and the two Marangoni stresses enter the instability threshold. A five-field weighted-residual model is then derived to describe finite-amplitude disturbances. The bulk and surface transport equations are written with compatible fluxes, which conserve their combined projected surfactant inventory in a periodic domain. The numerical examples show that solutal Marangoni stress suppresses disturbance growth and reduces the amplitude of the nonlinear waves. Thermal Marangoni stress increases the maximum growth rate, although its effect on the width of the unstable wavenumber band is different. Elastic memory changes both the onset and the finite-wavelength response. The nonlinear profiles develop a main hump and capillary ripples, accompanied by variations in bulk concentration, surface concentration, and interfacial temperature. These results describe the competition between thermocapillary forcing, surfactant redistribution and elastic stress within the retained long-wave model. The larger elastic parameters are interpreted as formal predictions of the truncated constitutive equations, rather than as a controlled extension to strongly elastic flow.
item.dc:creator: Sanghasri Mukhopadhyay, Severine Millet, Bastien Di Pierro, Asim Mukhopadhyay

item.title: Toward fully stabilized flow control using deep reinforcement learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.35676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study enhances the performance of flow control across various synthetic jet configurations by improving deep reinforcement learning techniques. The training results based on the foundational deep reinforcement learning framework indicate that as the Reynolds number increases, the effectiveness of synthetic jet control becomes increasingly sensitive to the position of the jet. When synthetic jets are positioned near the flow separation region, the control strategy consistently exhibits excellent performance. However, when synthetic jets are located farther from the separation region, the flow control performance diminishes, and the consumption of external energy increases. By enhancing dynamic state features and reshaping the reward function, we significantly improve control performance across various Reynolds numbers and synthetic jet positions. With the optimized framework, we achieve significant drag reduction effects ranging from 8% to 34% within the Reynolds number range of 100 to 400. The flow control strategy is capable of simultaneously achieving multiple control objectives, including reducing drag, suppressing lift, eliminating vortex shedding, and decreasing energy consumption. These findings highlight the potential of optimizing deep reinforcement learning frameworks to achieve more adaptive flow control strategies for various flow scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Wang Jia, Hang Xu

item.title: State-augmented deep reinforcement learning for active flow control around an elliptical cylinder
item.description: arXiv:2610.35731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We employ reinforcement learning algorithms to develop control strategies for manipulating synthetic jets on an elliptical cylinder, targeting robust flow control across varying aspect ratios (Ar). Our results show that for high aspect ratios (Ar = 1 and 0.75), the learned strategies effectively mitigate vortex shedding, achieving drag reductions of 13.4% and 20.1%, respectively. As the Ar decreases, more complex wake dynamics challenge flow control. For Ar = 0.5 and 0.25, drag reductions of 26.88% and 30.37% are achieved, though vortex suppression becomes increasingly difficult. For extremely slender cylinders (Ar = 0.1), we enhance control performance by enriching dynamic feature representation and using Kalman filtering for state estimation. Unlike conventional methods, our approach successfully achieves complete vortex shedding suppression, a maximum drag reduction of 32.2%, and eliminates periodic oscillations, stabilizing the flow. These results demonstrate the efficacy of state-enhanced RL in controlling highly slender geometries.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: International Journal of Heat and Fluid Flow 116, 109950 (2025)
item.dc:creator: Wang Jia, Hang Xu

item.title: Trapped sausage modes in magnetic pores: existence criteria and viscous damping
item.description: arXiv:2610.33251v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The conditions governing the existence and evolution of trapped sausage waves in photospheric magnetic pores are investigated, with particular emphasis on the limitations of analytical cut-off criteria and the role of viscous dissipation. A pore is modelled as a cylindrical magnetic flux tube with smoothly varying radial profiles of magnetic field and density, subject to the constraint that its temperature is lower than that of the surrounding atmosphere. For finite plasma-$\beta$, the linearised equations governing sausage-mode perturbations are derived, and an initial-value problem is solved numerically to obtain the full spatio-temporal evolution of the waves. The applicability of the analytical cut-off relation derived for a flux tube with step-function equilibrium profiles is examined, revealing that its predictions depend on the equilibrium parameters. The simulations reveal distinct wave behaviours across different parameter regimes, including the simultaneous excitation of trapped fast and slow sausage waves for a representative photospheric parameter set. Viscous damping is further investigated through the temporal evolution of the wave energy. Energy dissipation increases with decreasing viscous Reynolds number, increasing longitudinal wavenumber, and increasing radial magnetic-field contrast. These trends are consistent with enhanced viscous damping associated with increasingly fine spatial gradients generated through phase mixing. The findings highlight the importance of radial equilibrium structure in assessing sausage-wave trapping and demonstrate the sensitivity of wave-energy dissipation to the physical parameters of photospheric magnetic pores.
item.dc:creator: Zanyar Ebrahimi

item.title: Elasto-Plastocapillarity: Surface-Tension-Driven Flows of Yield-Stress Fluids
item.description: arXiv:2610.33345v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this perspective article, we introduce elasto-plastocapillarity: surface-tension-driven free-surface flows of yield-stress fluids in which capillary stresses compete with yielding and elastic relaxation. We frame the relevant parameter space, and highlight representative problems (drops, bubbles, jets/filaments, thin films, and porous media) that are central to applications ranging from additive manufacturing and coatings to biological flows. We then outline a set of timely open challenges, including surface-tension measurements, breakdown of scale separation near the microstructures, coupled bulk-interface flow experimental diagnosis, interfacial rheology and surface stresses, history dependence, constitutive models and boundary conditions, reduced theoretical models, and the emerging opportunity provided by artificial intelligence and microgravity; aimed at guiding future experiments, theory, and computation.
item.dc:creator: Maziyar Jalaal

item.title: CFL-aware edge design for graph neural solvers of hyperbolic transport
item.description: arXiv:2610.33769v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hyperbolic partial differential equations (PDEs) transport information at finite speed along characteristics, often producing shocks and discontinuities that are challenging to capture numerically. Graph neural networks (GNNs) offer learned update rules, but neighbor aggregation alone does not tell a GNN how far information must travel and along which edge. As a result, when a GNN model takes a time step larger than what was used in training, shock fronts smear and oscillations grow. In this work, we ask whether making the scale of transport explicit as an edge-local Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) signal can enhance GNNs' ability to model hyperbolic PDEs. Holding the architecture fixed, we vary only the information given to each edge, from a raw edge form to forms that progressively expose the edge-local transport interaction through direction, length, and wave speed. Because all of these are computed from the same ingredients, what changes is not the amount of information but its form. The results show a consistent pattern, in which feature count is not the limiting factor, and appending CFL directly to a raw edge form produces almost no benefit. The CFL conditioning proves most effective when the edge information already exposes the transport interaction, reducing final-step error by 10.4-14.4%, and the improvement widens as the step size grows larger. Notably, this improvement arises not from smearing the solution but from suppressing oscillations near shocks. These results point to a specific design principle that CFL conditioning is most effective when the edge representation already separates the direction of interaction from spatial scale, so that the CFL value has a well-defined quantity to modulate.
item.dc:creator: Jinyoung Jeong, Joseph B. Choi, Xinlun Cheng, H. S. Udaykumar, Sanghun Choi, Stephen S. Baek

item.title: Dynamic Interpolation and Higher-Order Turbulence Scales in 3D Navier-Stokes Flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.33911v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the three-dimensional unforced Navier-Stokes equations through the interaction between spatial analyticity and the geometric sparseness of regions of intense fluid activity (i.e., regions where the fluid's motion varies sharply). Interpreting higher-order derivative ratios as turbulence scales, we introduce time-weighted bridge inequalities that quantify the relationship between lower- and higher-order derivative norms. The time weights give the derivative ratios greater flexibility while ensuring that the resulting lower bound on the radius of analyticity dominates the sparseness scale of the super-level sets, indicating that the flow has entered the dissipation regime. Combining this scale comparison with a harmonic-measure maximum principle on one-dimensional sparse sets yields a contraction in the relevant derivative norm, thereby excluding a class of strongly turbulent blow-up scenarios. Consequently, the strong solution extends analytically beyond the candidate blow-up time.
item.dc:creator: Moses Patson Phiri, Zoran Gruji\'c

item.title: Microscopic Derivation of Stochastic Thin-Film Equation and Extensions to Two-Layer and Evaporating Films
item.description: arXiv:2610.35422v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While classical thin-film hydrodynamics models widely govern macroscopic fluid layers, they fail to capture the molecular-level thermal fluctuations that dictate nanoscale interfacial dynamics. Standard stochastic extensions rely on the long-wave approximation of the continuum fluctuating Navier-Stokes equations; however, this top-down paradigm lacks a formal connection to microscopic particle trajectories and cannot readily accommodate complex, non-equilibrium boundary mechanisms. We resolve this limitation by deriving the stochastic thin-film equation directly from the exact underlying N-particle Hamiltonian dynamics. This is achieved via a systematic, bottom-up coarse-graining framework based on a generalized fluctuating dynamic density-functional theory. Crucially, this first principles formulation offers unparalleled flexibility, enabling the seamless integration of multi-layered interfaces and non-conserved dynamics such as evaporation. For these complex configurations, our framework rigorously yields entirely novel stochastic thin-film equations featuring emergent noise terms that encapsulate microscopic fluctuations missing from classical top-down models.
item.dc:creator: Toby Kay, Serafim Kalliadasis

item.title: Interaction of Strong X-mode Waves with Magnetized Pair Plasmas
item.description: arXiv:2610.35849v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The interaction of strong ($a_0>1$), superluminal X-mode electromagnetic waves with magnetized pair plasma falls into two regimes set by $\varepsilon_{\rm B}\equiv a_0\omega_{\rm B}/\omega_0$, the ratio of the wave strength parameter to its frequency, in units of cyclotron frequency. For $\varepsilon_{\rm B}<1$ the wave propagates until induced scattering disrupts it. Using analytical theory and kinetic simulations, we show that the background magnetic field introduces a restoring frequency $\Omega_{\rm B}$ to scattering; when $\Omega_{\rm B}$ exceeds the scattering rate, the unattenuated length grows from $\simeq\varepsilon_{\rm p}^{-2/3}$ to $\simeq\varepsilon_{\rm B}^{1/2}/\varepsilon_{\rm p}$ wavelengths ($\varepsilon_{\rm p}\equiv a_0\omega_{\rm p}/\omega_0$; $\omega_{\rm p}$ is the plasma frequency). When $a_0^2>\varepsilon_{\rm B}>1$, the plasma current is nonlinear, and the wave is damped while riding a motional electric field, so one half-cycle appears attenuated. This framework has implications for the duration of fast radio bursts and whether they can escape their surroundings.
item.dc:creator: Navin Sridhar (Stanford University)

item.title: Reservoir computing based predictive reduced order model for steel grade intermixing in an industrial continuous casting tundish
item.description: arXiv:2509.26293v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continuous casting is a widely adopted process in the steel industry, where maintaining high steel quality is paramount. Efficient prediction of grade intermixing during ladle changeover operations is critical for maintaining steel quality and minimizing material losses in the continuous casting process. Among various factors influencing grade intermixing, operating parameters play a significant role, in addition to tundish geometry and flow control devices. In this study, three-dimensional, transient, two-phase turbulent flow simulations are conducted to investigate the ladle changeover operation. During this process, the molten steel level in the tundish typically varies over time, significantly affecting the grade intermixing phenomena. The influence of ladle change time on intermixing time has been presented. However, high-fidelity full-order simulations of such complex transient phenomena are computationally expensive and are impractical for real-time monitoring or design-space exploration in industrial-scale applications. To address this issue, a reduced order modelling approach based on proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and reservoir computing (RC) is employed to efficiently predict intermixing time. The proposed reduced order model (ROM) demonstrates excellent predictive accuracy using limited training data while requiring significantly less computational resources and training time. The results demonstrate the potential of the proposed methodology as a fast, reliable tool for real-time process monitoring and optimization in industrial continuous casting operations.
item.dc:creator: Harshith Gowrachari, Mattia Giuseppe Barra, Giovanni Stabile, Gianluca Bazzaro, Gianluigi Rozza

item.title: Thermodynamic selection of stationary Rayleigh-B\'enard flow states with slip and no-slip boundaries
item.description: arXiv:2510.05389v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multiple stationary flow states may exist under the same external/boundary conditions, while the hydrodynamic equations alone do not provide a global criterion for determining which of these states is preferentially selected. Here, we formulate and test such a criterion for stationary Rayleigh-B\'enard (RB) convection within a global non-equilibrium thermodynamic description (Ho\l yst et al., EPL 149, 30001 (2025)). We find that each stationary flow state in RB convection is characterized by the state function $\mathcal{F}=-E_k-\Psi$, where $E_k$ is the macroscopic kinetic energy of the flow and $\Psi$ is a thermodynamic state function that emerges from the nonlinear inertial term in the Navier-Stokes equation and is associated with the compression and redistribution of the gas accompanying the formation of the convective state. Changes in $\mathcal{F}$ correspond to path-independent work between stationary states. We show that, among dynamically accessible stationary states, the state with the lower value of $\mathcal{F}$ is more stable and is preferentially selected. Both the macroscopic kinetic energy acquired by the flow and the accompanying thermodynamic reorganization of the gas therefore contribute in the same direction to lowering $\mathcal{F}$ and stabilizing the stationary state. We test the criterion using numerical solutions of the hydrodynamic equations for Rayleigh-B\'enard convection with both slip and no-slip boundary conditions. For both types of boundary, the observed selection of competing stationary states is consistent with the thermodynamic prediction. The resulting state function provides a global criterion for the selection and stability of stationary hydrodynamic states. It establishes a direct connection between the nonlinear dynamics of the Navier-Stokes equation, thermodynamic work, and macroscopic flow stability.
item.dc:creator: Robert Ho{\l}yst, Pawe{\l} Jan \.Zuk, Konrad Gi\.zy\'nski, Jakub Wr\'obel, Anna Macio{\l}ek, Peter Vaughan Elsmere McClintock

item.title: Role of interchange and mixed modes in magnetic Rayleigh-Taylor instability dynamics --- a 2D vs 3D study
item.description: arXiv:2510.27053v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The magnetic Rayleigh-Taylor instability (MRTI) governs plasma mixing and transport in diverse systems. Owing to computational constraints, two-dimensional (2D) MRTI simulations are common. It is intuitive that 2D and three-dimensional (3D) counterparts differ significantly. One of the crucial differences is the types of wave modes admissible in the two systems. Perturbations in 3D MRTI facilitate the coexistence of interchange, undular, and mixed modes. Such rich physics is not possible in 2D, where the perturbations can only have undular modes. This raises the question, how do the interchange and mixed modes change the MRTI dynamics? To address this aspect, we simulate MRTI in 2D and 3D, across different magnetic field strengths. Consequently, this paper provides, currently lacking, a rigorous qualitative and quantitative evaluation of the similarities and differences between 2D and 3D MRTI. The 2D MRTI is characterized by large-scale plumes with inefficient mixing and significant fluid interpenetration, while the 3D is characterized by significant mixing and small-scale plumes. Consequently, higher gravitational potential energy is extracted in 2D. The small-scale vortices and large current sheets lead to higher energy dissipation in 3D. Extending to fundamental nature of evolution, 3D simulations tend towards a self-similar state (due to interchange and mixed modes). But such behaviour was not observed in our 2D simulations, due to the persistent influence of magnetic field. Surprisingly, the reconnection driven magnetic-to-kinetic energy conversion is similar in 2D and 3D. Overall, the work concludes that interchange and mixed modes influence the dynamics significantly leading to stark differences between 2D and 3D MRTI. The work thus guides the extent to which one can extrapolate the 2D simulations results to understand MRTI in astrophysical and fusion energy systems.
item.dc:creator: Manohar Teja Kalluri, Andrew Hillier

item.title: Maximum Velocity of a Liquid Metal Drop Driven by a Time-Dependent Electrocapillary Excitation
item.description: arXiv:2512.20516v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Gallium alloys are promising materials in biomedical engineering, electronics, and wireless communications, thanks to their good conductivity, non toxicity and their ability to sustain large deformations. They can be transported in capillaries using purely electric means by continuous electrowetting (CEW). Current models of CEW-driven flows do not address the transient response to fast changes in the excitation, crucial in many applications. Here, we present a theory that describes the CEW-driven oscillatory motion of a drop of Eutectic Gallium-Indium alloy inside a capillary. We consider inertia, viscosity and the transient response of the electrical circuit consisting of the drop plus the electrolyte where it is immersed. The theory describes fairly well the experimental drop velocity and explains the existence of an optimal frequency that maximizes the velocity.
item.dc:creator: Javier Otero Martinez, Ana Garcia Armada, Yi Li, Christian Nijhuis, Javier Rodr\'iguez-Rodr\'iguez

item.title: Data-driven reduced order model for residence time distribution analysis of an industrial-scale continuous casting tundish
item.description: arXiv:2601.00244v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The continuous casting tundish plays a critical role as a metallurgical reactor in the continuous casting process, with its flow characteristics serving as a key parameter in the production of high-quality steel. These characteristics are typically assessed through residence time distribution (RTD) curves. This study examines the flow behaviour in a single-strand continuous casting tundish through a combination of numerical simulations and experimental validation. Steady-state full order model (FOM) simulations are performed under both isothermal and non-isothermal conditions to evaluate the influence of thermal buoyancy on the velocity field, which is found to be negligible. The resulting flow fields are used to initialize transient tracer transport simulations for determining the RTD and flow volume partitioning. Subsequently, a data-driven reduced order model (ROM) is developed to predict the RTD response. Comparison of RTD curves obtained from experiments, FOM, and ROM shows excellent agreement, with the ROM accurately capturing the key flow characteristics at a fraction of the computational cost. These results highlight the potential of ROM techniques for efficient real-time analysis, design, and optimization of tundish operations in metallurgical processes.
item.dc:creator: Harshith Gowrachari, Mattia Giuseppe Barra, Giovanni Stabile, Gianluca Bazzaro, Gianluigi Rozza

item.title: Diffusion Model Driven Airfoil Design: From Geometry Encoding to Practical Applications
item.description: arXiv:2601.16228v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The diffusion model, the state-of-the-art generative machine-learning architecture, has shown promising results in airfoil inverse designs. In this study, we implement and trained a series of diffusion models on three different airfoil geometry data encoding formats -- principal component weights, ordered $x$-$y$ coordinates, and 2D signed distance functions (SDF) -- to generate 2D airfoils. By systematically comparing the performance of diffusion models trained on different data structures, it is found that for 2D airfoil design problems, the diffusion model performs the best when directly trained with coordinates. Training with latent space (principal component weights in this study) limits the model's design freedom and decreases the training effectiveness. Although the 2D SDF data appear to result in the least performing model, it proves its feasibility in aerodynamic shape generation, paving the way toward 3D problems where SDF is more favored. This study also investigated deploying the diffusion model in practical engineering applications. A multi-target optimization procedure is proposed based on the stochastic nature of the diffusion process, which drastically simplifies the procedure compared to conventional methods. The extrapolation performance of the model is also investigated by tasking the model with both aerodynamic and flow condition labels that are extrapolated beyond the training set boundaries.
item.dc:creator: Yingfan Geng, Jinhong Wang, Teng Cao

item.title: Weak Singularity of Navier-Stokes Equations Based on Energy Estimation in Sobolev Space
item.description: arXiv:2603.07574v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Based on Dou Huashu's energy gradient theory, this paper focuses on the weak singularity of the incompressible Navier-Stokes (NS) equations in steady, fully developed flows. When the gradient of total mechanical energy is perpendicular to the streamline (i.e., $ u_j \frac{\partial E}{\partial x_j} = 0 $), substituting this critical condition into the NS equations with no-slip boundary conditions leads to the viscous term $ \nu \to 0 $. To rigorously analyze the regularity of the solution, Sobolev space $ H_0^1(\Omega) $ is introduced for energy estimation. The results show that the velocity field loses $ H^1 $-regularity, and the NS equations degenerate into Euler equations, which admit discontinuous weak solutions. Thus, the position where the mechanical energy gradient is perpendicular to the streamline becomes a weak singularity of the NS equations.
item.dc:creator: Chio Chon Kit

item.title: Minimal seeds in the Stokes boundary layer
item.description: arXiv:2604.23213v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Minimal seeds are the smallest amplitude perturbations that trigger transition to turbulence in a subcritical flow. They are presented in the Stokes boundary layer, the oscillating flow of a viscous fluid above a flat plate, at a fixed initial phase corresponding to the timing of the Stokes boundary layer's optimal linear transient growth, at two moderate Reynolds numbers, and in two domains accommodating one and two wavelengths of the linearly optimal growing mode. Although the minimal seed trajectories are dominated by the flow's large linear transient growth at early times, only 77% of the initial energy is formed from the linearly optimal growing mode; the remainder ensures that nonlinear interaction transfers energy from spanwise- to streamwise- independent structures, and makes up for a timing mismatch between the end of linear transient growth and the production phase of the edge state (the saddle point separating the laminar and turbulent basins of attraction).
item.dc:creator: Tom Eaves

item.title: Lacunarity in a Two-Dimensional Atomizing Liquid Jet
item.description: arXiv:2604.26107v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Atomization stretches and folds the liquid--gas interface before fragmenting it into ligaments and droplets, making fractal measures a natural descriptor of the lacunarity of the final breakup state. We examine this idea in two-dimensional (2D) VOF-DNS of a liquid jet with adaptive mesh refinement in Basilisk. Box-counting of the full resolved interface does not yield a single scale-independent exponent. Instead, two scaling ranges appear, separated by a crossover near the box-counting level \(L_{\mathrm{box}}\simeq7\): coarser boxes measure the folded connected jet envelope, whereas finer boxes increasingly sample ligaments, droplets, and nearly smooth local interface segments. Decomposing the interface into detached droplets, ligaments, and the connected main body shows that the relevant effective dimension is structure dependent. Droplets are most lacunar with dimension below one, ligaments occupy an intermediate level, and the main body carries the largest coarse-scale dimension. This hierarchy persists over $Re_l=100$--$10^4$ at fixed $\We_g=200$. The lacunarity of droplets is reminiscent of that of the object positions in the night sky hypothesized by de Vaucouleurs.
item.dc:creator: Guangnian Ji, Yash Kulkarni, St\'ephane Zaleski

item.title: Physics-informed neural networks for shock capturing in inviscid flows around an airfoil
item.description: arXiv:2607.08130v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have shown promise in solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, shock capturing remains challenging for PINNs, particularly in steady flows around an airfoil, where shocks may not even be captured. In this study, we point out that the steady Euler equations used to construct the loss function impose weak constraints, which make it difficult to correct the continuous function approximation preference of neural networks, causing gradient descent to converge to a smooth local optimum. Based on this insight, we propose to strengthen the physical constraints by reconstructing steady shock capturing as a temporal evolution process governed by the unsteady Euler equations. The temporal evolution law of the flow field guides gradient descent, thereby alleviating its tendency to converge to smooth local optima and ensuring shock formation. We introduce a PDE loss function incorporating a pseudo-time stepping mechanism to obtain the steady state solution without solving the unsteady Euler equations over a long time interval. In addition, we develop a simplified formulation of the Euler equations to reduce the complexity of the PDE loss function, thereby improving shock capturing accuracy. By solving four forward problems involving different flow conditions and geometries, we verify that the proposed method achieves high accuracy in shock capturing while reducing the wall time to one-seventh of that required by existing advanced methods. Moreover, the proposed method demonstrates its capability to solve a parametric problem involving the angle of attack and Mach number without relying on any labeled data.
item.dc:creator: Jiahao Song, Wenbo Cao, Weiwei Zhang

item.title: Split Complex-Valued Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Forward and Inverse Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations
item.description: arXiv:2607.15087v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can solve forward and inverse PDE problems but may struggle with spectral bias and oscillatory, high-frequency, or phase-dependent solutions. We introduce a generalized split complex-valued PINN (SCV-PINN) framework with complex-valued parameters and latent representations. Split activations act separately on real and imaginary components while complex operations preserve their coupling, enabling amplitude--phase representations with practical optimization. Ablation studies evaluate split activation functions and collocation sampling strategies. Forward and inverse benchmarks include the Burgers, Allen--Cahn, Korteweg--de Vries, nonlinear Schr\"odinger, Helmholtz, and Poisson equations on regular and irregular domains; Kovasznay flow ($\mathrm{Re}=20$); lid-driven cavity flow ($\mathrm{Re}=100$); the Lorenz system; and inverse Burgers and Navier--Stokes problems ($\mathrm{Re}=100$). A three-dimensional Navier--Stokes Beltrami flow further demonstrates applicability to higher-dimensional nonlinear dynamics, with a relative $L_2$ error of $4.07\times10^{-5}$. Across these tests, SCV-PINN yields high-fidelity solutions and effective parameter identification, improving on real-valued PINNs and selected variants. The results suggest that split complex-valued representations can help address spectral-bias-related difficulties in nonlinear and oscillatory physical systems.
item.dc:creator: Biswanath Barman, Rajendra K. Ray, Debdeep Chatterjee

item.title: Label-Free Finite-Volume-Residual Training of Attention Graph Neural Networks for Coupled Thermo-Fluid Fields
item.description: arXiv:2607.20321v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural surrogates are widely used in scientific machine learning for fast prediction of three-dimensional (3D) thermo-fluid fields. However, generating training data using conventional numerical solvers often incurs substantial computational and storage costs. We propose to train an attention graph neural network by minimizing the finite-volume method (FVM) residuals of the governing equations. These residuals are evaluated directly on the mesh, requiring no labeled data. We evaluate the trained surrogates against computational fluid dynamics (CFD) references and a data-supervised baseline across four scenarios. On the two steady-state benchmarks, each solved on the same mesh as its CFD reference, the FVM-loss model reproduces the reference flow and temperature fields with mean field-averaged normalized root-mean-square errors (nRMSEs) near 3%, including the buoyancy-energy coupling. On the two parametric transient cases, the FVM-loss model attains lower rollout errors than the supervised baseline in almost every field, while avoiding the data-generation cost entirely. These results indicate that the FVM loss can provide a practical training signal for neural surrogates and reduce the model development cost.
item.dc:creator: Tianyu Li, Zhiwei Cao, Qingang Zhang, Ruihang Wang, Binyang Song, Yonggang Wen

item.title: Finite-Time Weak Singularities and the Statistical Structure of Turbulence in 3D Incompressible Navier-Stokes Equations
item.description: arXiv:2603.28308v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper provides a rigorous mathematical analysis of the global regularity problem for the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes (NS) equations, specifically addressing the conditions under which smooth initial data may lead to a loss of regularity. By departing from traditional phenomenological turbulence models and focusing strictly on the mechanical energy transport equation, we derive a fundamental critical condition, $\boldsymbol{u}\cdot\nabla E = 0,$ where $E = \frac12|\boldsymbol{u}|^2 + p$ is the specific mechanical energy, which characterizes the transition from laminar to turbulent flow.
item.dc:creator: Chio Chon Kit

item.title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for coupled stiff transport systems
item.description: arXiv:2606.21236v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN) struggle with stiff, regime-changing transport equations due to instability, loss imbalance, and violations of physical consistency. This paper investigates these failures through the Marshak wave equations, a canonical benchmark from radiative transport, where initial and boundary conditions differ by up to 12 orders of magnitude, and proposes modifications to the standard PINN framework to overcome them. Three modifications are introduced: a ScaledSigmoid final activation enforcing physical bounds and positivity of the unknowns; a logarithmic MSE loss replacing the standard quadratic loss for initial and boundary conditions, enabling training across extreme scale disparities; and explicit enforcement of global conservation laws as an additional physics loss term. Monte Carlo sampling with exponential time weighting is used throughout. The proposed framework recovers the Marshak wave dynamics - including the hot, cold, and wave-front regions - in good agreement with a reference Implicit Monte Carlo solution (sub-millimeter absolute error on the front position, although the relative error remains substantial at early times), with run times under 5 minutes. Ablation studies confirm that each ingredient is essential: linear activation, absence of the logarithmic loss, or removal of the PDE term each independently cause the method to fail qualitatively. This work identifies and resolves three concrete failure modes of standard PINN on stiff hyperbolic systems with nonlinear coupling. The combination of bounded activations, scale-aware loss functions, and conservation law enforcement constitutes a framework validated on the present one-dimensional Marshak wave problem, with potential extension to other coupled stiff transport systems in engineering.
item.dc:creator: Laetitia Laguzet, Gabriel Turinici

item.title: Precipitation-dissolution cycling drives intermittent salt creeping
item.description: arXiv:2607.11587v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Salt creeping --- the precipitation of salt crystals away from an evaporating liquid interface along surrounding surfaces --- occurs across settings from geology and cultural-heritage weathering to inkjet printing and carbon sequestration. Yet why its dynamics are sometimes smooth and sometimes violently intermittent has remained unexplained. Here we investigate the confined evaporation of salt solutions from a capillary with unidirectional water loss, and show that intermittent salt creeping is driven by a cycle of precipitation and dissolution sustained entirely by liquid transport. Time-resolved measurements reveal that each burst of crystal growth coincides with episodic imbibition of solution into the growing salt deposit on the outer capillary surface, which couples evaporation to crystallization. Combining experiments with a minimal theoretical model, we show that the difference between the supersaturation at which crystals nucleate and the saturation concentration at which they redissolve --- the metastable zone of the salt --- is sufficient to generate this cycle. The same mechanism accounts for the cases in which creeping is not intermittent: where the concentration at the capillary exit never reaches the nucleation threshold the liquid meniscus recedes smoothly, and where it cannot subsequently fall back below saturation the deposit grows continuously, exhibiting self-amplified creeping. Our results recast salt creeping as a relaxation oscillator, and identify precipitation-dissolution cycling as a generic route to intermittency in evaporating multicomponent fluids.
item.dc:creator: Javier Rodr\'iguez-Rodr\'iguez, Manikuntala Mukhopadhyay, Lijun Thayyil Raju, Detlef Lohse, Jasper van der Gucht, Uddalok Sen

item.title: Matrix-Free Resolvent Analysis for Large-Scale Aerodynamic Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.26931v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Predicting transonic buffet requires resolving both flow stability and disturbance amplification. Resolvent analysis gives the amplification. However, each gain needs the solution of tens of linear systems with the shifted Jacobian and its adjoint. Sparse direct factorization, the usual route, is extrapolated to need more than $130$ TB for a three-dimensional jet with $4\times 10^{7}$ unknowns. For the stiff Reynolds-averaged operator of a transonic wing, iterative solution has been reported to stall on the adjoint system. To avoid the direct factorization and to converge the adjoint, we present a matrix-free resolvent framework in the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes solver ADflow that combines automatic differentiation, Krylov solution with subspace recycling, and Lanczos bidiagonalization, with backward-error checks on each singular triplet. A three-level study of the NASA Common Research Model wing reaches $1.73\times 10^{8}$ complex unknowns. The coarsest grid predicts an unstable buffet mode, whereas no unstable eigenvalue is found on the finer grids within the shifts searched. The finer-grid gain peaks are consistent with collective amplification by damped modes, whose responses retain the buffet-cell structure and travel outboard at approximately $0.3$ of the free-stream speed. The peak gain remains sensitive to resolution despite these similar structures. These findings motivate future mesh adaptation targeted at convergence of flow stability and disturbance amplification.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Sunil Kanchi, Sicheng He

item.title: Strongly non-linear continuous model for wave propagation in 2D granular media: derivation and hyperbolicity analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.31738v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this work, we develop a nonlinear continuum model for wave propagation in two-dimensional granular materials, building on key ideas from Nesterenko's work. Starting from the Hertzian contact law and neglecting contact friction, we derive an effective continuum description through homogenization, assuming spherical, monodisperse grains, local periodicity, and the Cauchy--Born hypothesis. The resulting strain-gradient model depends on both the first and second gradients of the displacement field. We analyse the hyperbolicity of the leading-order system through its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, establishing conditions for hyperbolicity within a restricted deformation domain. The model is solved using an explicit finite-volume method to investigate gravitational settling and wave propagation. We derive analytical expressions for the longitudinal and transverse wave speeds and highlight their dependence on depth. Finally, the predictions of the continuum model are compared with existing discrete-element simulations. This formulation allows several extensions, including more complex packing geometries, contact laws, and large-deformation regimes in which the contact network can evolve.
item.dc:creator: Sebastiano Cominelli, R\'egis Cottereau, Sergey Gavrilyuk, Bruno Lombard, Fabien Petitpas
